Keywords: merge rebase integrate changes linear history preserve context
Description: Merge creates a merge commit preserving full branch history. Rebase replays commits on top of the target for a linear history. Both integrate changes — choose based on team preference and history clarity.
When to Use: Use merge to preserve full context; use rebase for linear clean history before merging
Command Example:
# Merge (preserves branch context)
git switch main
git merge feature/add-cors-middleware

# Rebase (linear history)
git switch feature/add-cors-middleware
git rebase main
git switch main
git merge --ff-only feature/add-cors-middleware
Gotchas: Never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared branch — it rewrites SHAs and diverges collaborators' history.

Keywords: squash merge PR clean history single commit pr
Description: Merge an entire feature branch as a single squashed commit onto the target. Keeps main history clean — each feature = one commit.
When to Use: In teams that prefer linear clean history on main — common GitHub PR workflow
Command Example:
# Squash-merge feature into main
git switch main
git merge --squash feature/add-cors-middleware
git commit -m 'feat(cors): add configurable CORS middleware'

# Or via GitHub PR: select 'Squash and merge' button
Gotchas: Squash merge loses individual commit authorship and granularity. The feature branch SHA is not in main history — deleting the branch loses the detail forever.

Keywords: conflict resolve merge rebase abort continue markers ours theirs
Description: When Git detects conflicting changes it inserts conflict markers (<<<<< ===== >>>>>) in the file. Edit files to resolve then mark with git add and continue the merge/rebase.
When to Use: Whenever git merge or git rebase stops with 'CONFLICT (content)'
Command Example:
# After conflict is detected
# 1. Open conflicted file and resolve markers
# 2. Stage the resolved file
git add path/to/resolved_file.py

# Continue merge
git merge --continue

# OR continue rebase
git rebase --continue

# Abort and undo
git merge --abort
git rebase --abort
Gotchas: Use a visual merge tool (git mergetool) for complex conflicts. Always test after resolving. A resolved conflict file that doesn't compile is worse than an abort.

Keywords: cherry-pick pick specific commit apply another branch hotfix
Description: Apply one or more specific commits from any branch onto the current branch. Creates new commits with the same changes but different SHAs.
When to Use: Backporting a bug fix from main to a release branch, or pulling a single commit from a feature branch
Command Example:
# Apply a single commit
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d

# Apply a range of commits
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d^..e4f5g6h

# Cherry-pick without committing (stage only)
git cherry-pick --no-commit a1b2c3d
Gotchas: Cherry-pick duplicates commits — the same logical change now exists in two places with different SHAs. This can cause conflicts later when the source branch is eventually merged.

Keywords: fast-forward merge ff linear no branch commit
Description: When main has not diverged from the feature branch Git can just move the pointer (fast-forward). Use --ff-only to require this — fail if diverged.
When to Use: After a rebase to enforce linear history — block merge if someone has added commits to main
Command Example:
# Force fast-forward (fail if not possible)
git merge --ff-only feature/my-branch

# Always create a merge commit (no fast-forward)
git merge --no-ff feature/my-branch
Gotchas: --no-ff always creates a merge commit even when fast-forward is possible. Some teams prefer this to preserve branch topology in history.

Keywords: rebase interactive reorder edit drop reword pick commits reorganize
Description: Use git rebase -i to reorder drop edit or reword individual commits. Change 'pick' to the desired action in the editor.
When to Use: Before merging to clean up a messy commit sequence — reorder fix-first commits or drop debug commits
Command Example:
git rebase -i HEAD~6

# In editor:
# pick  a1b2c3 feat: start feature
# reword d4e5f6 wip: temporary debug
# drop   g7h8i9 debug: remove print statements
# pick  j0k1l2 tests: add coverage
Gotchas: Drop irreversibly removes commits. Use git reflog within 90 days to recover dropped commits if needed. Always work on a copy branch first.

Keywords: strategy ours theirs recursive merge conflict resolution prefer
Description: Use -X ours or -X theirs to automatically resolve all conflicts in one direction during a merge or rebase.
When to Use: When you know definitively that one side is correct for all conflicts (e.g. applying a hotfix over outdated config)
Command Example:
# Prefer current branch in all conflicts
git merge -X ours feature/config-update

# Prefer incoming branch in all conflicts  
git merge -X theirs feature/config-update

# For rebase (reversed: ours=incoming, theirs=current)
git rebase -X theirs main
Gotchas: -X ours/-X theirs on rebase is reversed from merge. In rebase 'ours' is the incoming replayed commit and 'theirs' is the branch. This frequently causes confusion.

Keywords: abort undo cancel merge rebase in-progress reset recover
Description: Cancel an in-progress merge or rebase operation and return to the state before it started. Safe to use at any point during conflict resolution.
When to Use: When a merge or rebase went wrong and you want to start over or take a different approach
Command Example:
# Abort a merge
git merge --abort

# Abort a rebase
git rebase --abort

# Abort a cherry-pick
git cherry-pick --abort

# Check current state
git status
Gotchas: git merge --abort restores the working tree but only works during an active merge. If you made commits after starting use git reset instead.
